summary: Repaglinide is a short-acting meglitinide (glinide) insulin secretagogue used with diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes. It stimulates rapid, glucose-dependent insulin release for control of post-meal glucose. It is taken within 30 minutes before each meal, and the dose is skipped when a meal is skipped to reduce hypoglycemia. It is not for type 1 diabetes or diabetic ketoacidosis and is contraindicated with gemfibrozil.
indications: Adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus

moa: Repaglinide lowers blood glucose by stimulating insulin release from functioning pancreatic beta cells. It closes ATP-dependent potassium channels in the beta-cell membrane, depolarizing the cell and opening calcium channels; the resulting calcium influx induces insulin secretion. Insulin release is glucose-dependent and diminishes at low glucose concentrations. The ion-channel action is highly tissue selective with low affinity for heart and skeletal muscle.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to repaglinide or any inactive ingredient
Type 1 diabetes mellitus / diabetic ketoacidosis (not indicated)
relative: Concomitant use with NPH-insulin (not indicated; serious cardiovascular events reported)
monitor: Impaired hypoglycemia awareness (long-standing diabetes, autonomic neuropathy, beta-blocker use)

preg: Limited data from case reports and series have not identified a drug-associated risk of major birth defects or miscarriage. Teratogenicity was not seen in rats/rabbits at ~60 and ~1 times the maximum clinical dose. Poorly controlled diabetes in pregnancy carries substantial maternal and fetal risk; use only if clearly needed.
lact: Repaglinide is not recommended when breastfeeding (FDA label). There are no human data on its presence in milk.
renal: In severe renal impairment (CrCl 20-40 mL/min), start at 0.5 mg before each meal and titrate carefully. Repaglinide is not dialyzable.
hepatic: Use with caution in hepatic impairment; reduced metabolism may raise exposure. Use longer intervals between dose adjustments and monitor closely.

major: Clopidogrel — increases exposure 3.9-5.1-fold; avoid (if unavoidable, 0.5 mg/meal, max 4 mg/day)
Cyclosporine — increases exposure ~2.5-fold; limit to 6 mg/day
moderate: Strong CYP2C8/CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., clarithromycin, itraconazole) — increase levels; dose reduction may be needed
CYP3A4 inducers (e.g., rifampin, carbamazepine) — reduce levels/efficacy
minor: Drugs that may potentiate glucose lowering (NSAIDs, some antimicrobials, MAOIs); drugs that raise glucose (thiazides, corticosteroids, sympathomimetics)
interactions.food: Take within 30 minutes before meals; omit the dose when the meal is omitted.
interactions.alcohol: Alcohol may increase the risk and severity of hypoglycemia.
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor HbA1c and self-monitored blood glucose to guide titration.

serious: Severe hypoglycemia (may cause seizures, be life-threatening or fatal)
Serious cardiovascular events with concomitant NPH-insulin
emergency: Hypoglycemic coma, seizure, or other neurologic impairment

monitoring: Blood glucose (self-monitoring), especially with dose changes
Increased glucose monitoring in patients at higher hypoglycemia risk or on interacting drugs

missed: If a meal is missed, skip the dose for that meal. Do not take a dose without eating. Do not double doses.
overdose: Overdose may cause severe hypoglycemia with coma, seizure, or neurologic impairment — a medical emergency requiring hospitalization. Treat conscious patients with oral glucose; severe cases with IV dextrose. Monitor for at least 24-48 hours as hypoglycemia may recur. Repaglinide is not dialyzable.
